metadata.title: Why Zuckerberg and the 1% are signaling their health as the latest status symbol, and why you can't fake it with Ozempic

content.text:
Why Zuckerberg and the 1% are signaling their health as the latest status symbol, and why you can't fake it with Ozempic
Mark Zuckerberg is the 21st-century poster child for the 1%. At 42, Meta's CEO still gives off boyish, tech-bro energy. He can afford high-end toys and has plenty. After all, he's one of Forbes' Top five billionaires.
But in the past few years, he's set out to signal his status with strength, not stuff. Last year, he appeared on the Joe Rogan Experience podcast where the host praised the girth of Zuckerberg's neck as the two discussed the latter's martial arts training.
Must Read
-
Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one
-
Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP
-
The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes
"We're also lucky that you got into Jiu-Jitsu because I think that had an effect on you," Rogan said. "You look different."
Zuckerberg said having a solid neck was not only a "weapon" in martial arts, but part of his strategy for longevity as a corporate leader. He often posts videos of his workouts on Instagram.
Meanwhile, fellow tech billionaire Jeff Bezos is garnering similar attention for his before-and-after transformation from computer nerd to alpha male.
This wealth-health obsession is not just about the "masculine energy" that Zuckerberg says is needed in business today. As Time reports, wealthy women like Jeff Bezos's wife Lauren Sánchez Bezos are working out too, showing off their toned arms to the public.
A fit body has become one of the most popular status symbols of the 1% and, according to observers, there's more to the trend than meets the eye.
Why physical health is a status symbol in 2026
As Victor Ahonsi writes in Style Rave, the uber-rich face a unique 21st-century challenge when it comes to standing out.
Once upon a time (like, the late 20th century), the rich could demonstrate their wealth by sporting Rolex watches, strutting around in bespoke suits, clutching Hermès handbags or wearing expensive colognes.
But today, all those status symbols can be bought on credit or faked with cheap knockoffs. Meanwhile, AI and social media filters allow people to manipulate images and convey wealth that they may not have.
So, what's a rich person to flaunt? The one thing that can't be faked: exceptional physical health.
